title: Build, files and tools
goal: Run the program, know what each command and option does, where the data comes from, what each dictionary file holds, and how to measure a change.

blocks.x: What lyk is

lyk is steno with explicit word boundaries: every stroke after the first of a word carries a join key (`+`), so a stroke without it always starts a word. The program generates the dictionary (Plover JSON) from phonetic rules, starting from what Plover and Lapwing already do and measured against them. It is written in Rust with the rules as data. American English only. See [the join key](#/ref/join-key).
Main features

items: **Optimized for speed, not for being guessable.** A word's single-stroke outline comes from whichever source (a known brief, the phonetic rules, a brevity-ladder compression) costs the least to type. Nothing has to be derivable from the word's sound or spelling.

**One primary outline per word, extras only in free strokes.** A word has exactly one outline the theory teaches and fights for. Its other one-stroke forms (a Plover brief, the phonetic full form) are added last, only in strokes no other word needed, so they cost no other word anything.
**An explicit join key.** Continuation strokes are never mistaken for words, which is what lets a suffix be one key.

**Measured, not asserted.** `!build` and `!score` print cost and match-rate against Plover and Lapwing on the same words every time. The benchmark tables are in the repository README and are checked by `score --check-readme`.
**A miss always resolves.** A stroke the dictionary lacks still reads back as something sensible, as a real engine's last resort: see [the fallback](#/ref/fallback).

blocks.x: Commands
Run each as `cargo run --release -- COMMAND`.

head: Command
What it does
rows: Download the data into `data/` (safe to re-run).
How often the rules match Plover or Lapwing.
Check that the README's benchmark tables still match.
Rewrite any stale README table in place.
Briefs plus rules produce `out/lyk/02-lyk-*.json` (see [the files](#/ref/build-and-files/the-dictionary-files)), and print the cost.
Generate keymux's WASM fallback plugin from the rules (default `out/lyk-orthographic-fallback.rs`). See [the fallback](#/ref/fallback/keeping-the-plugin-honest).
`!build` plus `plugin`, copied straight into keymux's live config. Default destination `~/.config/keymux/steno/lyk`; override with `--to`.
Which rules wrote a word, next to Plover and Lapwing. Example: `explain moon`.
A word's family (`build`, `builds`, `building`...): each one's outline and its stem-plus-ending entry.
Every way to write a word as joined strokes, and what became of each. Example: `paths complete`.
Where the rules differ from Plover or Lapwing, for words of N syllables ranked after R. Example: `mismatches --syllables 2 --after 500`.
Which keys Plover and Lapwing use for each sound group. This is how most rules were found: it counts the keys they use where they agree.
Add a third dictionary to the cost tables. Example: `build --against magnum.rtf`.

A random quote, stroked in lyk next to Plover and Lapwing, a word that is not an entry composed from entries (see [how these commands answer](#/ref/build-and-files/how-quote-lookup-and-resolve-answer)).
A word, a phrase word by word, or (all capitals) a stroke, answered from the built dictionary. Example: `lookup "everybody's"`.
Read a stroke or `+`-joined run back as a word, as [the fallback](#/ref/fallback) does. Example: `resolve STKPW`. Use `--` before a run that starts with `-` or `~`: `resolve -- "-T/+-D"`.

blocks.x: `--rules FILE` and `--briefs FILE` make a command use your own rules and briefs.
Data sources

head: What
Source
rows: CMUdict (primary). For the words CMUdict has no entry for, the MFA US dictionary, then WikiPron US broad, translated from IPA (`src/ipa.rs`). Words with none of these use [spelling mode](#/ref/spelling-mode).
hermitdave/FrequencyWords (OpenSubtitles 2018). Each name's count is cut to a tenth so a name never outranks the word it sounds like (see [names](#/ref/collisions)).
Norvig's Google Books Ngrams (`count_2w.txt`), which picks the word pairs that become [phrases](#/ref/phrases).
Plover `main.json` and `commands.json`, and the Lapwing dictionaries.

blocks.x: The dictionary files

`!build` does not write one big dictionary. It writes several small Plover JSON files, one for each **way an entry came about**, and `!deploy` puts them in keymux's folder next to the reserved-stroke files. What a stroke means does not depend on the split.

head: File
What is in it
Entries (current build)
rows: each word's own outline: gold briefs, the plain rules reading, spelling and voicing variants, ladder-settled clashes, family members' shapes
long words written shorter by the brevity steps (`lead`, `fold`, `lean`, `ends`, `shell`, `skeleton`; see [how short](#/ref/brevity))
the `+`-joined fallbacks, composed from other words' own outlines (see [syllables](#/ref/syllables), [ways to join](#/ref/ways-to-join))
extra one-stroke ways to write a word, filling strokes nothing else needed (see [briefs](#/ref/briefs))
another pronunciation's outline for a word
two common words in one stroke (see [phrases](#/ref/phrases))

blocks.x: Alongside them in the same folder: `01-lyk-commands.json`, `03-lyk-punctuation.json`, `04-lyk-emilys-modifiers.json` (the [reserved strokes](#/ref/reserved-strokes), copied verbatim from `rules/reserved/`) and `05-lyk-orthographic-fallback.rs` (the [fallback](#/ref/fallback) plugin).

Two small files also land in `out/lyk/`, neither a dictionary and neither shipped by `!deploy`: `family.json` (which entries of `!words` are a family's shape, so a dictionary read back ranks them as the generator did) and `.built` (rewritten by every `!build`, even when no dictionary file changed, so the time says when the dictionary was last checked against the rules).

items: The generator keeps exactly one word per outline, so **no outline appears in two files** and the load order never changes what a stroke types. `!build` checks this.
Which file an entry goes in is decided in one place, `Role::of` in `src/output.rs`, from the entry's `Origin`.
The file name tells you what kind of outline you are looking at: a `+` outline in `backups` is a fallback, and the same word's primary is in `!words`.

keymux caches and reloads per file. A change that moves only some entries rewrites only those files, and `!build` compares bytes first, so a file whose content did not change is not rewritten and keymux sees nothing to do for it.

blocks.x: How quote, lookup and resolve answer

These three read back the dictionary `!build` already wrote to `out/lyk` instead of generating it again: a few seconds at most, not tens of seconds, and the same outline for every word (a test writes a build, reads it back and compares every word). If the rules or generator changed after the last `!build`, a note says so; `--rebuild` generates from scratch for that case. With no built dictionary they generate, as before.

items: **A word that is not an entry is composed from entries.** `everybody's` is not in the dictionary as one word, but `everybody` (`EFB`) is, and `'s` is a standalone suffix stroke (`+-PBTS`), so the answer is `EFB/+-PBTS`, two strokes, and is labelled `composed`. A word of two dictionary words (`noone`: `no` then `+one`) works the same way. The fewest strokes win, then the fewest keys, then the fewest pieces; the rules' syllable-by-syllable reading is used only if it costs less, and a tie goes to the pieces.
**The join key is written out.** Every stroke after a word's first carries `+`, in the rules' own readings too, as it does in the dictionary files.

**Plover and Lapwing get the same treatment.** Where a theory has no entry for a word, `quote` and `lookup` compose one from that theory's own words and its own suffix strokes (`{^s}`, `{^'s}`, `{^ing}`), with its `{^}` stroke between two words, since neither has a join key. A `-` in their column now means they genuinely cannot write the word that way.
A composition needs both pieces to be dictionary words of at least two letters (or a suffix after the first piece), so no stray letter is ever a "word".

blocks.x: Building and deploying

cargo run --release -- build     # writes out/lyk/02-lyk-*.json; prints each file and "(unchanged)"
cargo run --release -- deploy    # build + plugin, copied into ~/.config/keymux/steno/lyk

`!deploy` overwrites every generated file, then removes any `02-lyk-*.json` in the destination that this layout no longer writes. Files are sorted by outline and pretty-printed the same way every time, so the same dictionary always gives the same bytes.
Analysis tools

Python 3, no dependencies, in `tools/`. Every tool reads the built dictionary in `out/lyk/` (run `cargo run --release -- build` first) and the data in `data/`, from wherever it is run. `lyk_out.py` is the shared loader, not a tool.

head: Tool
What it answers
rows: Who holds an outline (`TKO*BG` is *dock*, in `!words`), or every outline a word has, fastest first. Quote outlines that contain a star.
What a change did: per-file entry and word counts, the words only one build has, and every word whose fastest outline changed, commonest first, with counts for the top 1,000 / 5,000 / 20,000.
How many words of two syllables or more can be joined in, by frequency band: one-stroke share, joined share, stem-plus-ending share, joined ways in per word (see [ways to join](#/ref/ways-to-join)).
Words still on a bare `/+*` marker, by band, real words against names, and who holds the plain and starred stroke each real word wanted (see [collisions](#/ref/collisions)).

The phrasing grammar ([lesson 19](#/lesson/19-phrasing-grammar), [lesson 20](#/lesson/20-phrasing-strokes)) as a trial folder to deploy and type: displaced entries, strokes saved on the corpora, a practice list.
Writes the data the lessons site runs on, and checks every outline the lessons and reference pages teach against the built dictionary. Exits non-zero on any wrong one.
Simulates letting phrases take strokes from words.

blocks.x: Measuring a change

cargo run --release -- build && cp -r out/lyk /tmp/before
# ...change the rules or the generator...
cargo run --release -- build && python3 tools/diff_builds.py /tmp/before

items: `cargo run --release -- score --check-readme` checks the README's tables.
To check that a change moved no word at all, compare a hash of the output: `sha256sum out/lyk/*.json`.
